title: TCP vs UDP: Reliable vs Fire-and-Forget
oneLiner: Same job -- get data from one program to another over IP -- two completely different guarantees about whether it actually arrives, in order, or at all.
keyTakeaway: TCP spends extra round-trips (a message there and a reply back) on a handshake, cumulative acknowledgments and automatic retransmission to give the application a RELIABLE, ORDERED byte stream: no gaps, duplicates or reordering while the connection lasts. It can still fail, with a reset or a timeout, and an ACK only means the peer's TCP got the bytes, not that the program on the other end processed them. UDP skips all of that and just sends -- faster and lower-overhead, but the receiving program has to handle loss and reordering itself, if it needs to at all.
explanation:
Both TCP and UDP sit at the Transport layer (see The OSI & TCP/IP Models) and both use port numbers to get data to the right PROGRAM once IP has gotten it to the right machine -- that's where the similarity ends. TCP is connection-oriented: before any real data moves, the two ends run a three-way handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) to agree the connection exists, then the receiver acknowledges the data it gets. ACKs are cumulative: each one names the next byte the receiver expects, which confirms every byte before it at once, so a receiver often sends one ACK for every two segments rather than one per segment. If the ACK for some data doesn't come back in time (or repeated ACKs for the same byte show a gap), TCP assumes a segment was lost and retransmits it, and the receiver holds later segments back until the missing one arrives -- so the receiving application reads a byte stream with no gaps, duplicates or reordering.

Two limits on that promise. An ACK means the other machine's TCP has received the bytes, not that the application there has read or acted on them; if the sender needs to know that, the application has to send its own reply. And the promise only holds while the connection lives: if retransmissions keep failing, or the other side resets the connection, TCP gives up and the application gets an error (a timeout or "connection reset"), without knowing how much of its last data the other application actually used.

UDP is connectionless: no handshake, no acknowledgment, no retransmission, no ordering guarantee. A UDP datagram is sent and the sender moves on, with zero built-in way to know whether it arrived.

That overhead buys TCP its reliability, but it costs latency (delay) -- the handshake alone is a full round-trip before any real data moves -- and makes TCP a bad fit for anything where a LATE packet is worse than a MISSING one. Live video/voice calls, competitive online games, and most DNS lookups use UDP for exactly this reason: a video call would rather drop one garbled frame and keep playing than pause and wait for a retransmit, which is exactly what TCP would force it to do. TCP is the right choice when correctness matters more than latency -- loading a web page, sending a file, anything where a missing or out-of-order byte would actually break the result.
